Butler County sits in south central Kentucky with Morgantown as the county seat. It is a small county with about 12,520 people based on recent Census estimates. The county sells delinquent real property taxes as certificates of delinquency through the County Clerk, not as tax deeds. This guide explains when Butler County tax sales are usually held, how registration works, what buyers should expect on sale day, and where to track official updates before you bid.

What is Butler County’s Tax Lien Investing System?

Butler County follows Kentucky’s certificate of delinquency system. That means investors buy the county’s tax lien claim on unpaid real estate taxes. They do not receive the deed at the county tax sale. The certificate acts as a lien against the property. In Kentucky’s normal schedule, county clerk tax sales are held between mid July and late August, though some counties can run later under special rules.

Important Details

Key Takeaways

  • Butler County, with a population of about 12,520, uses a certificate of delinquency system for tax lien sales, typically held in August.
  • Investors buy tax lien certificates, not property deeds, starting with 1% simple interest per month on the amount paid.
  • Participants must register before the sale, which takes place at the Butler County Clerk’s office at 9:00 a.m. local time.
  • Investing in Butler County offers lower entry costs compared to larger counties, making it ideal for tax lien investors.
  • Perform thorough due diligence to assess property value, access, and title issues before bidding.

Fun Facts About the County

  • Butler County’s recent population estimate is about 12,520.
  • The county has about 426 square miles of land.
  • Morgantown is the county seat and the county is part of the Bowling Green area.
  • General Butler State Resort Park is one of the best known local sites.

Attractions & Economic Highlights

  • Attractions: General Butler State Resort Park and the Butler Turpin House draw local visitors.
  • Transportation: I 165, US 231, KY 70, and KY 79 help connect the county.
  • Economy: The county promotes an industrial park, manufacturing space, and a regional business location near major routes.
  • Community: Butler County highlights small town living and active local events through community groups.

Why This County is Ideal for Tax Lien Investors

  • Butler County gives access to state tax lien opportunities through Kentucky’s lien sale system.
  • The statutory return starts at 1% per month, which is a strong gross yield compared with many basic savings options.
  • Entry costs can be lower than in larger urban counties because home values and rents are lower here. The county’s median owner occupied home value is $111,100 and median gross rent is $679.
  • For patient buyers, this can work as a low risk investment only when you study each parcel first.

Auction Process for Tax Lien Sales

Butler County’s tax lien auction is run by the County Clerk. Recent county notices show a 9:00 a.m. start and a required advance registration deadline. Kentucky also requires the clerk to advertise the sale and register third party buyers before the auction. Butler County usually holds the sale in August. A recent county page says the sale begins in September in most years, but the county’s posted sale notices and state schedules show August dates for recent sales. That tells investors to always trust the current sale notice first.

How the Auction Works

  1. Register first

    You must file the county registration form by the county deadline. Recent Butler County forms also required a copy of the state Certificate of Registration form, a business check, deposits, and fees.

  2. Priority claims go first

    If you already hold a prior year lien on the same property, Kentucky gives you first chance to buy the new year’s lien.

  3. Random order starts the rounds

    After priority claims are handled, the rest of the liens are sold in rounds. The picking order is set by random drawing.

  4. Buyers pick from their submitted list

    You can only select liens that were on the current list you turned in before the sale.

  5. Pay after the sale ends

    Your deposit is applied to what you bought. Any extra deposit is refunded within 10 business days after the sale.

Maximum Potential Returns and Expected Returns on Butler County Tax Lien Certificates

The basic return in Kentucky is simple interest of 1% per month on the amount paid for the certificate after purchase. That is about 12% simple annual interest before added costs and before any limits caused by payoff timing. On top of that, state law allows certain fees and some pre litigation attorney fees to be added within set limits. That can raise the amount collected when an owner redeems. Still, your real return depends on how fast the owner pays, whether the parcel has value, and whether legal enforcement is worth the cost. In Butler County, the better play is usually clean liens on marketable property, not just the highest face amount.

Open to All Investors / Foreign Investor Participation

The county materials reviewed do not limit participation to Butler County residents. The sale is open to registered third party purchasers who follow Kentucky rules and the county’s local registration steps. That means local buyers, out of county buyers, and out of state buyers can take part if they complete the required paperwork and deposits.

For foreign investors, the main issue is not county residency. It is paperwork, payment method, and handling notices, servicing, and legal follow up after purchase. Kentucky requires post sale notices and sets rules for later collection action. So overseas buyers should have a U.S. mailing plan, legal help, and a clear system for annual notices and records. That makes the process much easier.

Importance of Due Diligence in Butler County Tax Lien Investing

Good due diligence matters because you are buying a lien, not a house you can walk into the next day. A weak parcel can still create a weak investment even with a solid interest rate. Kentucky’s process can also lead to later foreclosure work through circuit court, which takes time and money.

What Due Diligence Entails

  • Check the parcel location, access, and use before bidding.
  • Review the amount due against likely property value.
  • Check whether the property seems occupied, vacant, landlocked, or damaged.
  • Search public records for title issues and other liens.
  • Know your exit plan if the lien is not paid quickly.

Risks of Skipping Due Diligence

  • You may buy a lien tied to land with little resale value.
  • Court action can cost more than the deal is worth.
  • A bad parcel can tie up money for a long time.
  • Marketability issues can hurt resale or recovery.

Buying Over the Counter Liens in Butler County

How to Purchase OTC Liens

Yes. Kentucky allows any remaining certificates of delinquency to be purchased after the county tax sale is finished. The state manual says unsold certificates may be bought at any time by any eligible third party purchaser. In practice, start with the Butler County Clerk and ask what remains available after the sale and what fees still apply.

Benefits of OTC Purchases

OTC buying removes sale day pressure. You can study the parcel first and buy only what fits your plan. There is no round based picking battle once the live sale is over. That makes OTC tax liens useful for buyers who care more about quality than speed.

Why Butler County is a Top Choice for Tax Lien Investors

Economic and Tax Advantages

  • Kentucky law gives a clear lien sale process through the County Clerk.
  • Butler County has road access through I 165 and US 231.
  • The county promotes industrial growth and regional access for business.

Real Estate Market Overview

Butler County is a smaller market. That can help careful lien buyers who want less competition than they might face in bigger counties. Census data shows modest home values and rent levels, which can support lower entry points. Still, every lien should be judged one parcel at a time. A small market can still hold weak lots, rough access, or low demand in certain spots.

Conclusion

Butler County is a county clerk tax lien market in Kentucky. Investors buy certificates of delinquency, not tax deeds. Recent county notices show an August sale pattern with a 9:00 a.m. start, advance registration, deposits, and county level rules that match Kentucky’s broader tax sale system. The return starts at 1% per month, and unsold liens may still be bought after the auction.

That said, smart investing here still comes down to careful research. Check value, access, title issues, and your collection plan before you buy. The county can be a good place to build a focused lien strategy, but only when you treat each parcel like its own deal.

Pro Tips

  • Focus on parcels near Morgantown or strong road access first. Rural access problems can ruin a good rate.
  • Use the county’s delinquent tax list and update it right before sale day. Kentucky allows taxpayers to pay up to the sale.
  • Build a short list, not a huge list. In round based picking, clean targets beat random volume.
  • Keep cash ready for deposits and final payment. Butler County’s recent form called for a business check.
  • Ask the clerk about unsold liens after the auction. OTC buying can be a calmer way to enter this county.

FAQs for Butler County Tax Liens

Do I get the property at the Butler County tax sale?

No. You buy a tax lien certificate, not the deed.

Can I renovate right after buying a lien?

No. You do not control the property at that stage.

Will I need quiet title?

Usually not after lien purchase alone. Quiet title issues come later only if you end up taking title through court action.

Can other liens still matter?

Yes. Always run your own title and court checks.

Can I resell the certificate?

Kentucky allows assignment of certificates with county recording requirements.
